newsitem.title: FRANCE: French govt says Socialists weakening EU commitment.
newsitem.headline: French govt says Socialists weakening EU commitment.

text.p: Ministers in France's centre-right government accused the opposition Socialists of watering down commitment to European integration on Tuesday as the nation began a snap parliamentary election campaign.
"The Socialists are in the depths of their heart very much in favour of building Europe and the single currency," Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told reporters.

"For electoral reasons they think they have to be less favourable, to mix a bit of water into their wine...it's a mistake," he said. Toubon was attending a speech by Prime Minister Alain Juppe to kick off his campaign for the May 25, June 1 vote.

Late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, in power from 1981 to 1995, was one of the architects of the Maastricht Treaty on European Union, along with Socialist Jacques Delors, head of the European Commission for a decade to the mid-1990s.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin has said the Socialists are committed to Maastricht and the planned single European currency from 1999 -- but not if it means a new bout of painful austerity.
Conservative President Jacques Chirac called the election on Monday, nine months early, saying France needed a renewed vigour and to prepare for the introduction of the single currency, the euro.

European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier also accused the Socialists of ditching the legacy of Mitterrand and said the election would help the EU by eliminating political instability in a major member state.
The snap vote means that the campaign will not coincide with haggling in the EU in early 1998 about which countries make the economic grade for economic and monetary union (EMU).
"A year of political uncertainty (in France) would be a real problem," he told Reuters.
Asked why the centre-right coalition was targeting the Socialists when they also back EU integration, he said:
"What I hear of the Socialists is that for mediocre electoral reasons they are throwing the European legacy of Francois Mitterrand and Jacques Delors out of the window."
"The treaty which we are taking on and which we will put into effect is Francois Mitterrand's treaty, with its strengths and weaknesses," he said.
In his speech, Juppe blamed the Socialist legacy for many of France's problems but did not mention the Socialists in the section about Europe.
"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union, everything to gain from Europe," he said.
